newsitem.title: UK: Orangemen urge N.Ireland Unionists to quit talks.
newsitem.headline: Orangemen urge N.Ireland Unionists to quit talks.

text.p: Protestant Orange Order leaders threw Northern Ireland's faltering peace process further into doubt on Monday when they called on all Unionist political parties to pull out of peace talks immediately.
Orange Lodge Grand Master Robert Saulters, speaking just 36 hours after the Irish Republican Army called a renewed ceasefire, described the peace process as a "poisoned chalice".

He called for "all Unionist parties to withdraw immediately in an act of unity and solidarity from the Stormont talks, the existence and purpose of which is to solely satisfy the insatiable demands of the republican agenda".

Saulters remarks came after the Orangemen, a strongly pro-British, Protestant organisation with branches across Northern Ireland, held talks with Unionist politicians, who also back British rule in the province.
The Orange Order has a strong influence in Unionist political affairs.
Unionists have been angered by the fact the IRA's ceasefire is expected to allow the guerrilla's Sinn Fein political spokesmen to join peace talks without the IRA being forced to turn in its weapons.

One of the smaller Unionists parties has already walked out of the talks, which are being held at Belfast's Stormont Castle, and the future of the negotitations depends of the reaction of the mainstream Unionist.
Northern Ireland's leading Unionist, David Trimble, told British Prime Minister Tony Blair that the IRA must start handing its arms in or peace talks will fail.
But Trimble, leader of the Ulster Unionist Party, stopped short of pulling out from the talks after the renewed IRA truce.
"We are not shirking our responsibilities. We are not in the mode of walking out," Trimble said after his Monday meeting with Blair.
But he faces a bitter dilemma.
Walk out and he risks being accused of torpedoing the best chance for peace in Northern Ireland where 3,200 people have died in 28 years of guerrilla conflict.

If he stays, Unionist hardliners will accuse him of selling out to IRA guerrillas fighting for a united Ireland. The gun will not be removed from Irish politics forever but just hidden under the negotiating table.

Trimble bluntly told Blair that the IRA must hand over some of its vast arsenal of bombs and guns so its political wing, Sinn Fein, can take part in talks. He has grave misgivings about the disarmament timetable.
Next to see Blair on Tuesday will be the Democratic Unionist Part, led by Ian Paisley. The DUP did not take part in Monday' session of the peace talks and have said they will not talk with Sinn Fein.
DUP deputy leader Peter Robinson told reporters: "The prime minister has to be told that the people of Northern Ireland do not accept IRA/Sinn Fein coming into a process holding onto their guns."
But Sinn Fein, which convinced the IRA it was worth calling a ceasefire, says the handing over of weapons should be part of a final settlement, not ongoing negotiations.
A plenary session of the talks on Wednesday votes on Anglo-Irish proposals that decommissioning of arms be tackled by a sub committee in parallel with political negotiations.
Trimble adopted a conciliatory line after his talks with Blair, telling Channel Four News: "We will still be there trying to resolve the problem."
Trimble had a blunt message for Sinn Fein and the IRA after the guerrilla group's second truce in under two years: "I want to hear from them that the war is over for good."

Sinn Fein negotiator Martin McGuinness said at the weekend that the IRA would not hand in a single bullet. By Monday he was still convinced the Unionists would not pull out of the talks despite the disarmament row.
"I don't believe David Trimble and the Ulster Unionist Party will walk out," he told Channel Four.
